England's Finest Roads for Motorcyclists

England may lack Scotland's wild remoteness, but it more than makes up for it with variety. From the steep mountain passes of the Lake District to the gentle sweeps of the Cotswolds, English roads offer something for every style of rider. Here are the roads that belong on every motorcyclist's bucket list.

The Lake District Passes

Hardknott Pass and Wrynose Pass are England's steepest roads, with gradients reaching 30%. These narrow, unfenced roads climb through spectacular Lakeland scenery and are a genuine test of skill. Ride them midweek to avoid the worst traffic. The sequence from Ambleside over both passes to Eskdale is one of England's most memorable motorcycle experiences.

Cat and Fiddle Road (A537)

The A537 from Macclesfield to Buxton is one of England's most famous biking roads. Flowing bends sweep across high moorland with panoramic views over Cheshire and the Peak District. The road has seen significant safety improvements including average speed cameras, but it remains a brilliant ride when ridden responsibly.

Snake Pass (A57)

Connecting Sheffield and Manchester, Snake Pass is a classic Pennine road that climbs to 512 metres. The road twists through remote moorland and can be atmospheric in low cloud. Winter closures are common, but from spring to autumn it's one of the Peak District's finest rides.

The best English motorcycle roads reward smooth, flowing riding rather than outright speed. Enjoy the scenery and respect the limits.

A686 Hartside Pass

The A686 from Penrith to Alston climbs to 580 metres at Hartside Top, making it one of England's highest A-roads. The ascent from the east offers sweeping bends with views across the Eden Valley to the Lake District fells. The Hartside Top Cafe (when open) is a legendary bikers' meeting point.

More Must-Ride English Roads

  • B3212 across Dartmoor — Open moorland, wild ponies, and ancient stone bridges
  • A170 through the North York Moors — Rolling countryside with sudden coastal views
  • A39 Atlantic Highway, Devon/Cornwall — Dramatic coastal road with sea views
  • B4632 Cotswolds — Honey-stone villages and gentle English countryside
  • Military Road, Northumberland — Following Hadrian's Wall through wild country

Seasonal Considerations

English roads are at their best from April to October. Spring brings fewer tourists and fresh green landscapes. Summer means longer days but heavier traffic, especially in the Lake District and Cotswolds. Autumn offers golden colours and quieter roads. Most mountain passes remain open year-round, though frost and ice can be hazardous from November to March.

Practical Tips

England's fuel station network is excellent — you're rarely more than 20 miles from the next one, even in rural areas. The road surface quality varies significantly; B-roads can have potholes and loose gravel. Always carry waterproofs and a high-visibility vest. faq.q: When are English roads at their best for riding?
faq.a: April to October is prime time. Spring brings fewer tourists and fresh landscapes, summer offers long days but heavier traffic in the Lake District and Cotswolds, and autumn delivers golden colours and quieter roads. Most mountain passes stay open all year, though frost and ice can be hazardous from November to March.

Hardknott Pass in the Lake District is the steepest, with gradients reaching 30%. Paired with the neighbouring Wrynose Pass, the sequence from Ambleside to Eskdale is one of England's most memorable and demanding motorcycle experiences. Ride it midweek to avoid queuing behind traffic on the narrow, unfenced sections.

faq.q: Are there many speed cameras on popular biking roads?
faq.a: Yes. Roads such as the Cat and Fiddle now use average speed cameras, and fixed cameras are common on other well-known biking routes. Ride smoothly within the limit, enjoy the scenery, and treat these roads as flowing rather than fast for the best and safest experience.

faq.q: How good is fuel availability in rural England?
faq.a: Very good. Unlike the Scottish Highlands, you are rarely more than 20 miles from the next fuel station, even in rural areas. That said, B-road surfaces vary and can carry potholes and loose gravel, so carry waterproofs and a high-visibility vest and plan sensible refuelling stops.
